# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic form of heart failure characterized by left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause [1]. The diagnostic criteria, refined by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group, define PPCM as heart failure with an LV ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45%, presenting in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum [2]. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion and a significant contributor to maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide [3].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography. It is notably high in Nigeria and Haiti, while estimates in the United States range from approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births [4,5]. Recognized risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, pre-eclampsia and other hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and African ancestry [6,7]. Registry data, including the global EORP PPCM registry, have improved understanding of regional differences in presentation and outcomes [8].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but appears to involve a "two-hit" model combining systemic predisposition with hormonal and vascular stress in late gestation [9]. A leading hypothesis implicates oxidative stress and the cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic fragment that impairs cardiac microvasculature and cardiomyocyte function [10]. Imbalance of angiogenic factors, particularly elevated soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) secreted by the placenta, links PPCM mechanistically to pre-eclampsia [11]. Genetic susceptibility is increasingly recognized, with truncating variants in *TTN* (titin) and other cardiomyopathy genes identified in a substantial proportion of patients, suggesting overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy [12,13].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

Symptoms of PPCM—dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, and peripheral edema—overlap considerably with those of normal late pregnancy, often delaying diagnosis [14]. A high index of suspicion is essential, particularly when symptoms are disproportionate or progressive. Echocardiography is the cornerstone of diagnosis, demonstrating reduced LVEF and frequently LV dilation [2]. Natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) are typically elevated and aid in distinguishing PPCM from physiologic dyspnea [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may assist in excluding alternative diagnoses and assessing myocardial tissue characteristics [16]. Importantly, thromboembolic complications are common owing to the hypercoagulable state of pregnancy combined with LV dysfunction [17].

## Management

Management of PPCM largely follows standard guideline-directed heart failure therapy, with modifications for pregnancy and lactation [18]. Before delivery, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated due to fetal toxicity; hydralazine and nitrates are preferred for afterload reduction [19]. Beta-blockers, preferably beta-1 selective agents, are generally safe and recommended [18]. After delivery, standard therapy including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists should be initiated [2].

Bromocriptine, which inhibits prolactin release, has emerged as a disease-specific therapy. A pilot randomized trial and subsequent studies suggested improved LV recovery when added to standard care, with anticoagulation recommended during treatment [20,21]. The German multicenter trial supported short-term bromocriptine regimens [22], though guidelines note that evidence remains limited and recommendations vary [18]. Anticoagulation is advised for patients with very low LVEF, atrial fibrillation, or evidence of intracardiac thrombus [17].

For patients with severe, refractory disease, mechanical circulatory support and, in selected cases, cardiac transplantation may be required [23]. PPCM is a notable indication for ventricular assist device support and transplant among young women [24]. Wearable cardioverter-defibrillators may offer temporary protection against sudden death during the recovery period, given the potential for spontaneous improvement [25].

## Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies

PPCM has a more favorable prognosis than many other cardiomyopathies, with a substantial proportion of women recovering LV function, often within six to twelve months [26]. Recovery rates differ by region and ethnicity, with poorer outcomes reported in some populations [27]. Baseline LVEF and LV dimensions are important predictors of recovery [28].

Counseling regarding subsequent pregnancies is critical. Women who have not recovered LV function face high risks of clinical deterioration and death with another pregnancy, whereas those with normalized function still carry meaningful, though lower, risk [29]. A pre-pregnancy assessment, including contractile reserve evaluation, is recommended to guide individualized counseling [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a potentially life-threatening but frequently reversible cause of heart failure in young women. Advances in understanding its hormonal and genetic basis have informed both diagnosis and emerging therapies such as bromocriptine. Early recognition, prompt guideline-based treatment, multidisciplinary care, and careful counseling regarding future pregnancies remain central to improving outcomes.
